purpose: Ruxolitinib is used to treat certain blood disorders like myelofibrosis and polycythemia vera, which cause your bone marrow to not work properly. It is also used for graft-versus-host disease, a condition that can happen after a stem cell transplant. A cream form is used to treat a skin condition called vitiligo and mild-to-moderate eczema (atopic dermatitis).
how_it_works: Your body has proteins called JAK enzymes that send signals telling cells to grow and multiply. In some diseases, these signals get stuck in the 'on' position and cause problems. Ruxolitinib blocks these overactive JAK enzymes, helping to calm down those signals and reduce symptoms like an enlarged spleen, itching, or skin discoloration.
common_side_effects: Bruising or bleeding more easily than usual, feeling tired or dizzy, headache, low blood counts (which can increase infection risk), weight gain, high cholesterol, urinary tract infections, and with the cream form — acne or a burning sensation at the application site.
warnings: This medicine can lower your immune system, making it harder to fight infections — including serious ones like tuberculosis or shingles. It may increase your risk of blood clots, heart attack, stroke, and certain cancers including lymphoma and skin cancer. Do not stop taking it suddenly without talking to your doctor. Tell your doctor about all medications you take, as many drugs can interact with ruxolitinib. Avoid grapefruit while taking it. Women who are pregnant or breastfeeding should not use this medication.
typical_dosing: For blood disorders taken as a tablet, the usual starting dose is 5 mg to 20 mg taken by mouth twice a day, depending on your condition and blood counts. Your doctor will adjust your dose based on how you respond. The cream (Opzelura) is usually applied to the affected skin areas twice daily. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
